title: Jared Kushner’s Strategic Pixie Dust
excerpt: For reasons known only to himself, the normally enigmatic Jared Kushner—who, together with Steve Witkoff, another wealthy real-estate guy, does most of the Trum
body: For reasons known only to himself, the normally enigmatic Jared Kushner—who, together with Steve Witkoff, another wealthy real-estate guy, does most of the Trump administration’s heavy-duty negotiations—has opened up
In a post on X on November 22, and a lengthy interview with Mathias Döpfner of Axel Springer, he has laid out his thoughts about the talks with Russia and Ukraine
Kushner’s comments are revealing in unintended and often uncomplimentary ways
To begin with, there is his truckling to Vladimir Putin and his henchmen
Putin is a “grand master of politics,” Kushner said

This will be news to the bereaved families of 700,000 Russian dead, the even larger numbers of those permanently maimed, the population suffering shortages of gas and groceries, and the million-odd émigrés who fled their country

Kushner also described the lead Russian negotiator, Kirill Dmitriev, a man of reptilian smoothness, as “an incredible friend,” and the Russian national security adviser Yuri Ushakov as “fantastic.” The sycophancy toward Moscow does not end there

Russia, he explained, has done the West a great favor by agreeing “not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing.” The war did not result from Russia’s brutal decision to destroy the Ukrainian state and dismember it, but rather “bad decisions and miscalculations by many leaders over the years.” Russia needs to be convinced that “NATO is not seeking confrontation,” and Putin, who is “a historic figure,” has “a very deep understanding of the issues” and “wants peace.” Meanwhile, Kushner’s attitude to America’s allies is distinctly cooler
He claimed that the Ukrainians blew up an earlier phase of the negotiations by attacking one of Putin’s homes—which the CIA assesses they did not

The White House, he insisted, has not put any pressure on Ukraine by withholding intelligence or weapons (or, presumably, access to Starlink and Starshield): “That’s a lot of misinformation.” President Trump’s call for elections in Ukraine was both a defense of democracy and a pushback at Volodymyr Zelensky’s criticism of the White House—Trump is “a very strong counterpuncher,” after all

America’s NATO allies do not come off well: “There’s a lot of fear in Europe that’s unfounded,” he said, ignoring assassinations real and attempted, and potentially lethal sabotage conducted by the Russian secret services
The Europeans were excluded from peace talks in Abu Dhabi “because President Putin sees a lot of provocative statements out of Europe and a lot of provocative actions out of Europe

And so his view is he does not see that they are ready for peace.” Who, Kushner asked, could blame him? One key to Kushner’s view is a throwaway line: “This isn’t about fairness or who’s right or wrong.” To the contrary, this is about a war in which the distinction between aggressor and victim, predator and prey could not be clearer
For that alone the ghosts of Bucha and a thousand other massacres and cruelties perpetrated by Russia should haunt his sleep, but one doubts they will
That Kushner can say and believe these things is bad enough
No less stunning is his hubris, and that of the other members of the administration

The X post, the interview, and other statements indicate that the administration wishes for nothing less than a redesign of “European security architecture,” a grand settlement of the kind that Lord Castlereagh, Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord, and Klemens von Metternich concocted after the Napoleonic Wars, and that a no less acute group of statesmen—Dean Acheson, Clement Attlee, and Konrad Adenauer—devised after World War II
One of the leading aspirants for the role of master geopolitical architect is Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense who insists that the time has come for NATO 3.0

At a conference of the Ukrainian Defence Contact Group in Brussels on November 17, he denounced Ukrainian strikes on Russian infrastructure—the kind of thing the United States recently did to Iran—as being militarily valueless
He then walked out of the meeting before the Ukrainian defense minister could give a classified briefing on the war, including, presumably, Kyiv’s deep-strike campaign

Colby, who sat through the meeting with the Trumpian pout masquerading as scowl that characterizes so many administration officials, convinced some German observers that he too sympathized far more with Russia than with Ukraine

The German defense minister, Boris Pistorius, a man of few but choice words, merely observed that such criticisms of Ukraine were “quite a stupid thing.” Part of the inanity of these proceedings is that Kushner, Colby, and other officials believe that they can reshape Europe’s security arrangements while (1) sympathizing with its enemies, (2) denouncing America’s allies, and (3) serving an administration that repeatedly insists on its intention to withdraw as much as possible from European commitments, when it is not actively discussing seizing some of Europe’s territory
To moral blindness, then, add political idiocy

But there is something even deeper at work, a profound unseriousness that is rooted not merely in ignorance of history and indifference to the actual circumstances of the greatest act of international criminality in this century, but faith in magical diplomacy
It is a vision of peace through strategic witchcraft

The tell here is in Kushner’s X post: He floats the idea of “a credible Article 5–like guarantee, backed by deterrence and deconfliction arrangements,” saying that President Trump would agree to such an offer for Ukraine only if it were “highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked.” It sounds at first blush like a grift: Make promises only under the condition that you know you will never have to fulfill them
Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty guarantees nothing, an inconvenient truth long obfuscated by American and European rhetoric

It states that “an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all,” but it promises reactions by any country only “as it deems necessary.” If, say, the United States does not deem it necessary to defend Ukraine from another Russian invasion, it would not be obliged to
For much of the Cold War, “deterrence” was the strategic pixie dust that was supposed to keep Europe safe
Early on, at least, it was bolstered by substantial conventional forces on the ground

At one point, for example, the British Army on the Rhine was larger than the entire British Army today, while the Bundeswehr had half a million men and women under arms, 12 divisions, and a thousand aircraft—and behind those forces, American nuclear superiority and more than a quarter million U.S. troops on the ground
Guarantees without the ability to deliver on them, though, are as meaningless as those Great Britain gave to Poland in the summer of 1939
They deter nothing, because deterrence is the by-product of the ability and will to fight, not a thing unto itself

The irascible Admiral Jacky Fisher, the dyspeptic and histrionic first sea lord in turn-of-the-century Britain, was closer to the truth when he said (at a peace conference in 1899, no less): What you call my truculence is all for peace

If you rub it in, both at home and abroad, that you are ready for instant war with every unit of your strength in the first line, and intend to be first in, and hit your enemy in the belly, and kick him when he is down … then people will keep clear of you
Fisher spoke partly for effect and went further than any sane or even ethical leader might, but he had a point
At least he did not live, as Jared Kushner and Elbridge Colby apparently do, in a world of amoral, vapid, and self-serving geopolitical delusion.

title: The Good Old Days of American Spy Movies and TV
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture

ET on November 27, 2026 Spies, at least for now, are back in the public eye: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond—I’ve said all I’ll say on that — and the Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, confessed to canoodling with an alleged Chinese-intelligence asset, so we’re thinking about espionage again
But after the Cold War, with a few notable exceptions, including the eternal 007 series, the entertainment industry lost interest in spies for the most part
On television, they have reemerged only in occasional treats such as the wonderful Slow Horses , a series about a bunch of dedicated but often incompetent MI5 operatives
And that’s too bad, because the days when spies were everywhere in American culture were a blast
The heyday of pop-spy mania ran from the early 1960s to about the mid-1970s

Some of these offerings are well worth revisiting, not only as entertainment but also as fascinating cultural artifacts of an era when America was leading the free world in the fight against the Kremlin. (Given the current state of U.S. foreign policy , you can imagine why I am nostalgic for such times.) During that spy craze, American culture mostly imported products from the spy-thriller mother country, the United Kingdom. (As early as 1954, CBS ran the first television adaptation of an Ian Fleming novel, a version of Casino Royale that features an American James Bond—named Jimmy Bond, I kid you not—played by Barry Nelson.) But the cultural obsession with spies really took off in the mid-1960s, by which point Sean Connery had established 007 as an international film hero
Why were we so infatuated with espionage during the swingin’ ’60s? The Cold War obviously had a lot to do with it
Americans for the first time faced an enemy superpower, but in the atomic age, when the price of war was too high, they had to fight their opponents in the shadows
This era of spies was also a product of the liberated mores of the times
Movies, especially, were allowed to be racier, and spy flicks soon featured handsome cads cheerfully engaging in plenty of sex and violence
Bond and his colleagues represented a new image of virility and savoir faire, freed from the uptight 1950s
But they also defiantly rejected the more progressive changes of the ’60s
These new spies had a license to kill, to use women like toys, to drive like maniacs, to gamble, to drink, and to do anything else a manly man thought was necessary to save the world
British spy shows, more grounded in the reality of European espionage, were generally grittier and less flashy than the Hollywood-ized Bond movies
Some of them, however, were sexed up when exported to more gung-ho U.S. viewers
From 1960 to 1961, for example, Patrick McGoohan played John Drake on Danger Man , an agent who works for some nebulous NATO intelligence agency
As Bond mania grew, the series was revived in 1964, losing some of its film-noir elements in favor of more 007 influences
Drake was moved over to British intelligence, the show was retitled Secret Agent for U.S. syndication, and Johnny Rivers performed a new theme song that became a ’60s classic

After Secret Agent ended its run in late 1967, McGoohan followed it up in 1968 with The Prisoner , a kind of spy-fi (spy-and-science-fiction mash-up) series about an agent who tries to retire and is sent to a secret halfway house for wayward spooks
The series, which is still a cult favorite, calls his character only “Number Six”—but we all knew it was Drake
Likewise, when The Avengers premiered in the U.K. in 1961, it was mostly a pedestrian private-eye show
But soon, it turned into a spy-fi romp, with John Steed (Patrick Macnee) and his female colleague Mrs
Gale (Honor Blackman) as the agents who served Queen and country
In a case of spy-fiction cross-pollination, Blackman left to play Pussy Galore in Goldfinger , the 007 adventure about a plot to blow up America’s gold reserves in Kentucky

After Diana Rigg arrived as Steed’s new partner, Emma Peel, the show winked at the audience: In a 1965 episode, she hands Steed his mail, including a Christmas card from Gale. “How nice of her to remember me,” Steed says. “What can she be doing in Fort Knox?” The next year, the series was snapped up by America’s ABC, and Rigg, in her leather catsuits , and Macnee, in his bowler hat and Pierre Cardin suits, became spy-fiction icons

Spies quickly flooded U.S. television screens after what must have been an endless stream of high-concept pitches: “James Bond, but in the old American West as a Secret Service agent, against supervillains with names such as Dr
Loveless and Count Manzeppi.” ( The Wild Wild West .) “James Bond, but as an incompetent boob in a comedy.” ( Get Smart! ) “James Bond, but he’s a Black American tennis coach.” ( I Spy

The series’ co-star, Bill Cosby, now lives in shame, but back in 1965, it was groundbreaking to get Americans to accept a Black man as a hero instead of a sidekick.) The Man From U.N.C.L.E. , a show that first hit TV screens in 1964, was spy-fi from the start
Not only was it derived from the Bond successes, but Fleming reportedly helped develop an early pitch for the show; U.N.C.L.E
Agent Napoleon Solo was even named for a Bond character

Solo and his Soviet partner, Ilya Kuriakin, work for U.N.C.L.E., a kind of international superagency that battles the psychos from T.H.R.U.S.H., an obvious stand-in for Fleming’s baddies, SPECTRE. ( U.N.C.L.E. producers came up with these names because they sounded hip; they filled in what the acronyms meant later.) The Americans had their own homegrown spies, too

In 1966, Mission: Impossible premiered on CBS featuring a team of operatives so secret that the U.S. government hides their instructions on a tape recorder in a telephone booth or a vending machine and other wacky places, after which the tape self-destructs into a hissing, smoky mess. (The Tom Cruise Mission: Impossible reboots, much like the Jason Bourne movies, are fine as generic action flicks, but for some Cold War spy fun, treat yourself to the original series.) Even cartoons got in on the act

Everyone remembers Bullwinkle’s enemies, Boris and Natasha, and you might remember Secret Squirrel, but do you remember Cool McCool, a 1966 Saturday-morning secret agent drummed up by Bob Kane, a co-creator of Batman? Probably not, and that’s fine, because Cool McCool is terrible. (But not as terrible as “Lancelot Link, Secret Chimp” a 1970 spy spoof for kids that had a cast of, yes, live chimpanzees.) Eventually, the spy craze got out of hand, as all fads do

James Coburn and Dean Martin both signed up for spy spoofs, and saw varying results: Coburn’s two outings as Derek Flint, an agent of Z.O.W.I.E. (don’t ask), are fine, but Martin’s Matt Helm movies are unwatchable—at least they provided some raw material for Mike Myers when he created Austin Powers
After the 1960s, the cynical ’70s were upon us, and the fascination with spies dissipated
Events such as Watergate made government spookery seem a lot less admirable; in 1975, a congressional committee outed a lot of the CIA’s uglier tricks to the American public
Bond movies thrived, but 007 had much of the spy-genre field to himself at the theaters and on television
It was a great ride, and you can catch many of these programs on stations that run vintage TV shows, random YouTube channels , or a few streaming platforms
That’s your assignment over this holiday weekend, Agent Reader, and remember: This newsletter will self-destruct in five seconds

title: What We Got Wrong About Comas
excerpt: People in a coma, according to medical textbooks, cannot possibly be aware
body: People in a coma, according to medical textbooks, cannot possibly be aware
They cannot be roused by sound or smell or touch—or anything at all

When Brian Edlow, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, sees these comatose patients in the ICU, their brain injuries are in many cases so severe that recovery or even survival is not certain
And yet, after his team examined the brain activity of a comatose 80-year-old woman recently, she appeared to be responding to their instructions
Asked to imagine opening and closing her right hand, the woman’s brain buzzed with a pattern similar to that of a fully conscious person
The doctors confirmed the finding with two different methods: EEG, which detects brain waves via electrodes on the surface of the head, and fMRI, which tracks blood flow inside the brain
She is the first comatose patient to show signs of consciousness on both tests, which Edlow and his colleagues detail in a report published last month
The case of this 80-year-old woman adds to the nascent evidence that at least some patients in a coma are actually conscious

Using the EEG method, doctors at Columbia University in 2019 found eight comatose people—out of 56—whose brain activity suggested that they could respond to verbal instructions. “I remember reading that and just thinking, How is that possible? ” Edlow told me
That study inspired his own efforts to find consciousness in comatose patients

Varina Boerwinkle, a pediatric neurologist now at the University of North Carolina, has used fMRI to look for consciousness in comatose children—including one memorable 6-year-old boy she originally did not think would survive. ( He did , after the fMRI gave his parents hope to try a subsequent surgery.) Every day, Boerwinkle told me, she teaches medical residents who are “understandably incredulous” that comatose patients might hear and understand what is being said in their room

All of these findings build on the earlier discovery of consciousness in a different group of patients—those who are in vegetative or minimally conscious states, which are gray zones between coma and normal consciousness
Unlike people in a coma, these patients have eyes that open and flick around the room
They look “awake” but are still physically unresponsive
A significant fraction of such patients, perhaps a quarter, exhibit consciousness on EEG or fMRI tests, according to a landmark paper published in 2024
I profiled the family of one patient, Ian Berg, last year
He was diagnosed as vegetative after a car accident 40 years ago, but his mother never stopped believing he was still conscious inside
But the detection of consciousness in coma is both more surprising—comatose patients do not even look awake—and in some ways more pressing
Coma is by definition a short-term phenomenon, which ends in one of three outcomes
Patients can regain consciousness, recovering fully or with some level of disability, from minor to significant
They can enter a long-term vegetative or minimally conscious state
Or, if their injury is too severe, they can die

During the days or weeks a patient is in a coma, their family faces the agonizing choice of continuing aggressive medical care for an uncertain outcome or discontinuing care, which will have a certain outcome: death
In a study of several trauma centers in Canada, 70 percent of brain-injury deaths resulted from withdrawal of care
Some of the patients, the recent research suggests, could have been conscious when they died
How should the discovery of consciousness affect life-and-death decisions for ICU patients? Those who exhibit consciousness on EEG go on to have better recoveries, according to the Columbia study
Nearly half of unresponsive ICU patients with consciousness recovered enough to follow commands by the time of discharge; only a quarter of those without consciousness did

Their divergent trajectories held 12 months later too. (That analysis pooled all unresponsive ICU patients, whether comatose, vegetative, or minimally conscious.) Covert consciousness is therefore a good sign for recovery, but Jan Claassen, the Columbia neurologist who led that study, warns of overinterpreting the results
A negative test does not mean that a patient cannot recover, he told me
In the seven years since the report was published, Claassen has continued to investigate better ways of predicting recovery from coma or testing for consciousness via EEG
Even at his ICU, though, these tests are not routine clinical practice
In fact, very few ICUs in the United States look for covert consciousness
Edlow’s hospital had examined the 80-year-old woman as part of a pioneering Emerging Consciousness Program he launched in 2022

If she had shown up at an average hospital, neither her doctors nor her family would ever have learned she was likely still aware. “Coma has been a dehumanizing condition,” Claude Hemphill, a neurologist at UC San Francisco and co-chair of the Curing Coma Campaign, told me
In the ICU room, doctors and families might speak over a comatose patient or act as if they aren’t there

These recent findings deepen the case for small but telling actions Hemphill takes to acknowledge the patient, such as sitting next to their bed or looking back and forth when speaking with their family
Even for doctors open to the possibility of consciousness in coma patients, testing for it is logistically difficult
An fMRI machine is big and expensive, and moving a severely ill patient inside one can prove challenging
Even EEG, a more portable technology, can be tricky to perform or interpret for doctors unfamiliar with testing for covert consciousness

A third technology called fNIRS, which works by shining light through the skull, is being investigated by Adrian Owen, a neuroscientist who found the very first vegetative patient with covert consciousness back in 2006

title: Why College Towns Are Booming
excerpt: Berkeley, California, a quintessential university town, may well be the birthplace of anti-growth politics
body: Berkeley, California, a quintessential university town, may well be the birthplace of anti-growth politics
In 1916, local reformers adopted the country’s first single-family zoning, prohibiting apartments in most residential neighborhoods as a way to exclude disfavored minorities
Progressives would carry on this legacy for the next century in the name of protecting residents from unwanted development

Beginning in the 1960s, housing opponents tried to block construction on environmental grounds—and eventually argued that new residents qualified as “pollution.” Permitting rates were anemic for decades, keeping the city’s population flat even while enrollment at UC Berkeley skyrocketed
By the mid-2010s, Berkeley ranked as one of the most expensive college towns in America

But around that time, it began to undergo a remarkable reversal, as students, staff, and young faculty at UC Berkeley came to realize that housing shortages hurt their interests and began working together to push for more inclusive policies

In 2017, they helped organize the group East Bay for Everyone, which showed up constantly to public hearings and helped elect a city council aligned with the “Yes in My Backyard” movement then emerging statewide
With the aid of new state laws loosening zoning requirements—some of which I advocated for as part of my work at YIMBY organizations—permitting of new housing surged
As of 2024, nominal rents barely exceeded 2018 levels, despite inflation
Today Berkeley represents a major success for the YIMBY movement, and it’s not the only one
Across the country, college towns have become boomtowns
As longtime strongholds of progressive politics, their evolution from NIMBY holdouts to YIMBY hotbeds serves as a testament to the left’s shift on housing

If the movement’s next decade is going to deliver on the promise of its first, my fellow housing advocates nationwide will have to replicate the methods that allowed college towns to so quickly build and become more affordable. [ Jonathan Chait: The misguided Democratic opposition to permitting reform ] One obvious lesson is that students and young academics can be persuasive advocates
These groups tend to be temporarily poor and highly social and to have flexible schedules
To put this in criminological terms, they have the motive, means, and opportunity to show up in numbers at the weekday public hearings that determine what does and doesn’t get built

As a result of such activism, once-stagnant college towns across California, including San Luis Obispo and Santa Cruz, have undergone similar transformations as Berkeley: Permitting is up, and rents are starting to stabilize or sometimes even fall
At UC San Diego, campus advocates successfully pushed for new on-campus high-rises that will house thousands of students, helping alleviate the state’s extraordinary rate of student homelessness

In many college towns across the country, off -campus housing is proliferating too: Real-estate-investment trusts, often known as REITs, have plowed billions of dollars into student housing, building roughly 35,000 beds in 2024 alone
According to an estimate from 2020 , some 12 percent of all rental units are for students
Throughout the United States, college towns have taken steps to allow for greater housing density, as Ann Arbor, Michigan, did last month
Perhaps the most extreme example of this is Austin, where the flagship campus of the University of Texas is located
After a decade of trying and failing to overhaul the city zoning code, local YIMBYs began to get their way in the late 2010s, when increasing demand for housing kicked off a construction frenzy
A local backlash grew , threatening to upend the reforms that were turning Greater Austin into America’s fastest-growing metropolis

But YIMBYs were able to preserve their progress thanks in large part to one key group. “When students started to show up to Austin city-council meetings and endorse candidates based on their housing policies, and generally make it clear they want to be viewed as true constituents, it was a game changer,” Felicity Maxwell, a board member of a local pro-housing organization , told me

In 2023, with strong support from local students, lawmakers in Austin were able to sustain the city’s home-building surge by ending both single-family zoning and minimum off-street-parking requirements
The city has been building so much housing that rents are down , even as migration continues to soar
Students and junior academics cannot change decades-old urban-planning habits on their own
Senior faculty have also been instrumental in dislodging a kind of progressivism that treats all development as predatory
Well - respected professors have repeatedly called attention to the need for more housing, drawing on a growing scholarly consensus on the issue

Leaders in more and more college towns have come to see exclusionary housing as incompatible with liberal politics. “I was troubled by the tensions between Ithaca being a progressive, welcoming community that was also staggeringly unaffordable,” Robert Cantelmo, the pro-growth mayor of Ithaca, New York, told me
Cantelmo is a product of Cornell University, where he received a master’s degree and later helped lead a research center
During his tenure, Ithaca has had more active cranes than many far larger American cities
A similar story has played out in Cambridge, Massachusetts
In 2022, a recent MIT grad named Burhan Azeem mobilized students at his alma mater, who in turn helped him become the youngest councilor in the history of the city

Azeem became vice mayor earlier this year and has led a successful campaign to legalize Paris-scale density citywide. [ Read: A perfectly crude way to solve America’s housing shortage ] “Cambridge is one of the youngest towns in Massachusetts, and not just because of undergraduates,” Azeem told me. “A lot of people stay here after graduation, or stay on for years in graduate school, and their big question is, Will I ever be able to buy a home here? That makes for a natural pro-housing constituency.” In some places, however, college communities have limited political influence
At Stanford University, 98 percent of undergraduates live on campus, which is just outside Palo Alto’s municipal limits, leaving them effectively iced out from politics in that city
UC Santa Barbara is located in a county of nearly 500,000 residents, which even the most organized students would struggle to sway
In other college towns, such as Gainesville, Florida, intransigent homeowners and state governments have thwarted reform
Moreover, there are reasons to think that the college-town boom may be short-lived
University enrollment is headed for a death spiral , and dozens of colleges are closing each year

title: Gift Guide for the AI Apocalypse
excerpt: A cataclysm that destroys all human life is bad for many reasons, among them the resulting uselessness of a gift guide
body: A cataclysm that destroys all human life is bad for many reasons, among them the resulting uselessness of a gift guide
Setting aside an extinction scenario , the more interesting—and more likely—outcome of an AI apocalypse is one in which ordinary life continues, but changed
This is closer to the biblical sense of the term apocalypse , which means a pulling back of the curtain on a divine truth
And of all the ways to prepare for an apocalypse brought about by artificial intelligence, surely the most American would be to go shopping
Before we start, here are the rules of this AI-apocalypse shopping spree
First, the calamitous scenarios (and the giftable baubles!) must be specifically connected to artificial intelligence
A backup generator and a supply of nonperishable foods would be useful in all sorts of situations: natural disasters, conventional warfare, climatological stress, terrorism
But owning them makes you a prepper of a more generic stripe
You can find lots of gift guides of those sorts in other types of publications
Second, the gifts need not attempt to prevent an apocalyptic outcome from arising—as if that would even be possible—nor solve a calamity once it does
The wares we seek will not avert AI ruination, but they should help curtail its impacts in a meaningful way

Perhaps more important, pondering the gift ought to help elucidate the threat itself—and reframe our understanding of what counts as an AI calamity in the first place. [ Read: Prepare for the AI apocalypse like you’d prepare for a snowstorm ] And finally, a good AI-apocalypse gift ought to be handy now, in advance of civilization-scale doomsday
The forces that might lead to bad outcomes live in the present as much as the future
Gifts for the Loss of Shared Reality The internet has undermined truth for decades now
Blogs and social-media platforms offered an alternative to the gatekeeping of traditional media
They democratized expression but also fragmented communities
Eventually, everyone’s ability to say anything all the time helped erode the institutional authority of science and the government
Accuracy became less important than engagement
These incentives industrialized misinformation, making fabrication profitable
Personalized feeds mated to algorithmic recommendations accelerated the culture of conspiracy theories
AI threatens to eradicate the fragments of truth that remain
Misinformation used to spread by accident, simply because billions of people could say anything online
Then disinformation duped people on purpose
But AI has installed automated and personalized synthetic text, images, video, and audio absolutely everywhere
Humankind risks suffocating in so much seemingly real but actually fake information that the distinction between the two might become erased
Reality can’t be brought back entirely, but some tools can help

The Leica M-11P is a digital camera that includes hardware-authenticated digital signatures to verify the images it creates, including a record of their provenance and changes that have been made to them
The device is somewhat bulky and extremely expensive
A physical negative offers material evidence of what the camera saw
Reality Defender is a software service that uses a variety of methods to detect AI manipulation in images, audio, and video
The service is intended for corporate and industrial use at a cost of about $400 a year for 1,000 scans a month, but a free plan offers 50 image analyses each month
A print-newspaper subscription is a fixed, physical version of the daily or weekly news that allows you to hold the same information as your friends and neighbors
It also offers a record of what was reported at a given time, unperturbed by questionable summaries, screenshots, or social-media posts
Gifts for the Collapse of Expertise Artificial intelligence offers an effective solution to almost any intellectual or practical problem
It can compose an email, write a job application, tell you what to eat for dinner, build a stock portfolio, offer instructions for servicing a septic tank
Or, better put, AI can appear to offer such solutions, cheaply and instantaneously
As more people and organizations take AI outputs as presumed expertise, the people who possess actual expertise in any subject could become displaced
People may stop learning how to do things for themselves—or they may come to trust the confidence of a machine, delivered effortlessly, more than they trust other people
Unlike reality, expertise really is something you can purchase, by hiring people with knowledge, experience, and credentials to carry out tasks or offer advice
This might be a graphic designer, a structural engineer, a turf-lawn-management expert, an accountant, or a tutor in a specialized subject

title: How cutting-edge prosthetics can help probe the human mind
excerpt: Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson
body: Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson
There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi
He sustained a horrific injury as a teenager, which left him paralyzed and without a left hand
Today, he uses his own experience to guide his practice as a trauma therapist
He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand
Unlike standard prosthetics, this one connects directly to nerves in Avi’s arm
He literally has wires coming out of his arm to plug it in with
Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech
But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently, for things like drinking from a cup (which is not easy ) and writing (also not easy )
What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself
He has learned how to use something like seven different prosthetics in the 17 years since his accident
By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job
He had surgery to implant electrodes in his arm and will eventually need another to remove them

And he won’t even get to keep the latest prosthetic long term. “While it’s unfortunate at times, and irritating at times, I do not regret what has come from [the accident], or the fact that it happened,” he told me. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.” The research team at the University of Utah that is running the trial hopes it will answer longstanding questions about the technology
How does it fare in a real-world setting, outside of the lab? What do people end up using it for? Where can improvements be made? There may be some surprises along the way
Avi has found that his prosthetic wrist can feel sore and stiff when it’s been overused, just like his flesh-and-blood wrist
Weirdly, that feeling can be relieved by stretching it out
What’s going on here? No one really knows
Scientists don’t know whether Avi’s brain will change as a result of using the bionic hand, either
Before the trial started, they performed brain scans to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain

Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs—how might a bionic limb affect their brains? Avi will have the device until late January 2027 at the least, and potentially for another year
It will depend on how the research is progressing, how Avi feels, and how much funding the team can secure
As a result, it’s not clear how long the device might even be expected to last in a person’s body
I’ll be following this study, though, and will keep you posted

title: Will we ever see another game like GTA VI?
excerpt: Grand Theft Auto VI arrived last week, 13 years after the last installment in the series, to an enormous debut — nearly $3.8 billion in its first day, according
body: Grand Theft Auto VI arrived last week, 13 years after the last installment in the series, to an enormous debut — nearly $3.8 billion in its first day, according to developer Rockstar Games
That’s more than Avengers: Endgame has earned at the global box office across its entire theatrical run, including rereleases
The game took more than eight years to develop, and Rockstar grew to more than 4,700 employees worldwide during production

In the game, players are catapulted into Leonida, a fictional version of Florida that includes Vice City, the series’ take on Miami.  Unlike past games in the series, you play as a couple, Jason and Lucia, who are trying to make enough money to support their young family and make it out

Maintaining their relationship is just as important as robbing stores or completing missions.  For all that GTA VI is shaping up to be a critically acclaimed triumph, however, it arrives at a difficult moment for the video game industry
Studios have endured years of layoffs and rising development costs, while workers worry about how generative AI could affect their jobs and creative work

Can an industry under this much pressure afford to keep making games this big, or is GTA VI doomed to be the last of its kind? To find out, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Chris Plante, a video game journalist with about two decades of experience and host of the podcast Post Games
They discussed GTA VI’s long road to release, what could be next for the franchise and whether DLC is on the horizon, and the future of blockbuster gaming more broadly
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  Chris, people are saying that this game is the last of its kind
Why are they saying that? It kind of is, but I think we should be really specific when we say that

The last of its kind means the last of this: thousands and thousands of people trying to make one game without artificial intelligence, and it being a historic, all-consuming moment.  The best shot that we have of another game like this happening is GTA VII
But what I would be wary of is saying there aren’t going to be big-budget video games anymore

If you look at another game that came out just this month, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a remake of one of the most famous games ever, one of the most beloved games ever, and it looks stunning
And it cost a fraction of what Grand Theft Auto cost [to make]

And yet it still feels absolutely decadent.  You know what a fair comparison would be? We get those Avatar movies — they take forever because they cost a fortune to make, they require all this new technology
But you wouldn’t look at an Avatar and say, ‘Well, they’re never going to make expensive movies anymore.’ We still get Dune

There is a whole separate question about the stability of the highest ends of the industry, the companies that tried to be the Grand Theft Autos: Electronic Arts, the company that makes Madden; companies like Xbox, which owns Activision, which makes Call of Duty.  You might notice I’m saying a lot of which does this but owns that
The consolidation in the industry is real, and it’s a real problem
So there’s going to be turmoil, but it is not the end of video games, and it’s not even the end of big video games
It sounds like this is a great time for the industry, but it’s actually the opposite
It’s a great time for people who play video games and a nightmare time for people who make video games
If you play video games right now, you can turn on Steam, which is a storefront on PC, and you can find literally hundreds of games that were released just this week
Over a thousand new games are released every month on Steam
And because of that, it targets not every niche, but close

There is probably something out there for you.  This is a nightmare for people who make games because even Grand Theft Auto, when it comes to PC, is going to live right alongside all those other games

So for the people who do not have the name recognition, who do not have the marketing, you can launch a game that you spent tens, maybe hundreds of millions of dollars on, and it is going to, the same day that it comes out, compete against a brand-new $5 game that was made by three or four people with a whole bunch of contractor support for a very low cost and has just as good of odds, minus the marketing, of being a hit

Is AI going to make it less risky for big gaming companies to invest in developing something ambitious because maybe they can make it dramatically cheaper and compete with the games that only cost $10 to develop? AI, as the investment class has it in their head: The answer is no, not whatsoever.  “Looking even beyond games, there’s a lot of reason to be cautious about things that seem like they’re going to make things faster actually, in the long term, making them much slower.” AI as a tool, it gets more complicated

I think when a lot of people hear AI, they think, I’ve seen a video where I can go on Google and type a prompt, and I say, give me Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but make it like a Black Eyed Peas concert
And people are like, wow, you seem really out of touch, but I’ll make it for you anyway
And then you have this great game, and you are getting the party started in here
And that is not how any of this works at all
My former colleague, Frank Lantz, who’s an educator and game designer, would compare it to art, if you also had to build a skyscraper or a highway
You have to both make the architecture and make the art
We do not have this world where games just are going to materialize.  Now where it gets really complicated and it gets really messy inside the industry is using AI tools for things like coding
And this is very controversial amongst a certain corner of video games culture and video game developers

There are people who want a full ban, that we are not using AI on anything, that we need to protect jobs, and that it shouldn’t be used for generating images or art or music or code.  And then there are people who say, but I use AI for code

I think it is relatively common, and that is somewhat of a controversial take, but it is what I hear from so many people I talk to who are on that side of game development, to be using it when you are programming as a tool

I think there’s a lot of promises, but I think that, again, looking even beyond games, there’s a lot of reason to be cautious about things that seem like they’re going to make things faster actually, in the long term, making them much slower

And we still live in a world where it makes sense to start developing a GTA VII? It does for Rockstar for sure, though I don’t think that they will be in a rush to do it anytime soon, for a few reasons.  One, they still need to get Grand Theft Auto Online out

title: The last refuges for endangered animals are becoming disaster zones
excerpt: When the Mariana crow calls, it’s taken as a warning.  To the Indigenous CHamoru people of the Mariana Islands, the bird is known as the Åga, an ancestral
body: When the Mariana crow calls, it’s taken as a warning.  To the Indigenous CHamoru people of the Mariana Islands, the bird is known as the Åga, an ancestral messenger who alerts the community of impending illness or weather disaster

In the dense canopy of Rota’s limestone forest, where the Mariana crow lives, it is a gardener — a key seed disperser from which the lush canopy grows.  According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service , the species is endemic to Guam and the nearby island of Rota, a US territory, which means they live nowhere else on Earth
But over the past 60 years, they have vanished from Guam and dwindled on Rota
Now teetering on the brink of extinction, every remaining Mariana crow represents a fragile ecosystem and a deep cultural lineage the islands cannot afford to lose

Researchers from the University of Washington and ecologists from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance are working tirelessly to make sure that doesn’t happen.  The effort to prevent the bird’s precipitous decline in the wild has been underway for more than two decades
Beginning in 2005 with field monitoring and observation, researchers realized they would have to step in and raise the birds in human-assisted aviaries to save the species
By 2016, teams collected their first clutch of wild eggs and successfully released the first cohort back into the forest the following year

In the years since, the active recovery program has bred dozens of birds in captivity and has given the wild population a boost that researchers hope the birds can eventually sustain on their own — all made possible through millions of dollars in federal grants and academic funding, decades of field research, and tight coordination among local and federal partners.  But in July, the entire effort was endangered by one of the most drastic events to hit the region in years
For days, Category 5 Super Typhoon Bavi pummeled the island
As it barreled down, conservationists realized they needed to act fast and save the species, so they assembled makeshift indoor aviaries inside the scientists’ quarters on the research base
The small crew boarded up windows and stocked up on food
Only weeks into their new lives in the forest, the crows were back inside
Their caretakers would ride out the storm beside them.  The decision saved the flock.  The team successfully brought 13 birds to safety before the storm hit
Of the nine that weren’t captured, two died, and one was emaciated and had a minor wing injury from the storm
The rest of the wild population took a hit, too, though researchers are still accounting for the total loss
The toll on the ongoing conservation work was profound

Bavi obliterated the facility’s outdoor aviaries, leaving an exhausted crew to care for the agitated Mariana crow in a compound that still remains without power just as another storm, Category 4 Typhoon Champi, passed through the islands in mid-October.  Ecologist Sarah Faegre, the primary investigator for the University of Washington’s Rota Avian Behavioral Ecology Program, was there to assess the damage
The enormous aviary, which her own father, an architect, built more than a decade ago, had survived its fair share of typhoons

But last month, it lay collapsed. “It was heartbreaking,” she told me. “It nearly made me cry.” The massive, industrial-grade plastic pipe frame that held the aviary together, Faegre said, “looked like a pile of broken bones.” Around the world, countless endangered animals are a single disaster from absolute collapse.  Decades of habitat loss, shifting climate and degrading ecosystems have pushed much of the planet’s biodiversity to precariously low populations

But advances in science and conservation have yielded remarkable recoveries: The Endangered Species Act alone has clawed back nearly 300 species — the bald eagle, humpback whale, and grizzly bear among them — from the precipice.  Still, the survival of many more animals today faces a dangerous bottleneck — sometimes it’s just a single aviary, a small team of researchers, and a modest pot of funding that stands in the way of extinction.  At the same time, shifting political tides threaten to undermine those efforts even further

In the US, the Trump administration has slashed the very funding that could help an effort like breeding the Mariana crows recover from a major storm. “If we’re no longer able to access funding and take action to do restoration work, it’s less likely that the species will ever recover and be able to be removed from the [endangered species] list,” said Sara Gottlieb, with the Nature Conservancy.  With such existential challenges, it’s worth questioning why Faegre and others are so dedicated to saving the Mariana crow population

But in late October, even in the midst of Bavi’s aftermath, the research team discovered something hopeful.  A precarious moment The Mariana Islands, a 15-island archipelago that includes the US territories of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, are regularly hit with tropical storms

But for generations, the Mariana crow was able to persist in the remote, northern island of Rota — a model of a small, resilient ecosystem in part because its geography has protected it from the most severe disasters. “Rota and the Mariana crow have seen many typhoons throughout history and have proven resilience,” said Phillip Hannon, research coordinator for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance’s Mariana crow rear-and-release program. “The jungle, too, regenerates very quickly in the heat and humidity of a tropical island.”  But as climate change has fueled more frequent and severe storms, even the historically buffered areas are more exposed than ever

And this year, abnormally warm ocean temperatures in the Pacific have caused an unusual clustering of typhoon activity this year .  Why I reported this story I was born and raised on Saipan in the Northern Mariana Islands, a US territory just north of Guam, where military presence was simply a backdrop of growing up
But long before concrete runways carved up our native coral limestone, these islands thrived with unique flora and fauna that filled the forest canopy with song
Today, many of the species our ancestors knew survive mostly in oral histories and local legends — the kinds of stories I grew up hearing

Centuries of colonial expansion, military construction, and the escalating climate crisis have fractured these isolated ecosystems, quieting once-bustling forests into fragments of their natural heritage
I wanted to tell this story because it is a rare hopeful one — even despite the ongoing threats to the restoration of the Åga
For the Mariana crow, the situation was already grave

The population was completely wiped out from Guam by the late 1990s and early 2000s after a new predator, the brown tree snake — introduced into Guam via World War II military cargo ships — devastated native nests

With Guam’s population gone, the species’ survival now hinges entirely on Rota, a 33-square-mile island north of Guam where severe typhoons repeatedly thrash the native forest canopy the species uses for nesting.  But intensifying super typhoons are striking an ecosystem already fractured by habitat loss and invasive species from rampant militarization
With every storm hitting an already diminished population, the work of conservationists is a crucial step to buy more time so that wildlife can eventually rebound on its own

The joint Mariana crow recovery project by the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance (SDZWA), the University of Washington, and local partners across Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands has boosted the population from its lowest — just roughly 130 individuals — to  300 birds, 79 of which were reared and reintroduced by SDZWA

But this conservation breeding approach is “a method of last resort” only used when a species is on the absolute brink of extinction, like the California condor or the Hawaiian crow known as ‘Alalā, said Ronald Swaisgood, director of recovery ecology at the San Diego Zoo. “All of these species absolutely depend on the critical habitat; otherwise, they’ll all be in breeding centers, and none will be in the wild,” Swaisgood said. “But sometimes that’s where we unfortunately finish because increasingly more species require this kind of infrastructure, which is very costly, but it’s our only remaining tool to prevent extinction of some of these species.” Although it might sound like a long shot, many of these last-resort strategies have had real success
In East Tennessee, ecologists successfully recovered the Smoky Madtom
In the 1980s, decades after the tiny, nocturnal Smoky Madtom catfish was accidentally wiped out of its native creek, a researcher named Gerry Dinkins rediscovered a fragile surviving population

With the help of federal funding, scientists gathered a handful of wild eggs during the summer spawning season, brought them back to the lab to incubate, then nurtured the fragile fry in specialized aquariums, away from predators and other threats

Once the young madtoms were strong enough to fend for themselves, they carried them back to their native home in Abrams Creek, slipping them into the water at night to match their nocturnal habits and keep hungry birds and larger fish at bay
Decades of work to save a species can unravel in a single disaster Saving a species from extinction can take decades
A single storm or wildfire can put that work in jeopardy

title: Robots could transform breast surgery forever
excerpt: “Wait, I can feel that?” Ami Brasure remembers thinking
body: “Wait, I can feel that?” Ami Brasure remembers thinking

For most of us, the experience that dazzled her couldn’t be more ordinary: You’re standing around, maybe in your kitchen or living room, drinking something a little too carelessly, and before you know it, the liquid is dribbling down your chin and trickling down your chest — and you can feel it
It’s a familiar sensation (in this case, perhaps an embarrassing one)

But for Brasure, a 50-year-old retail sales manager from the Washington, DC, area, it was life-affirming.  At the time, she was recovering from a double mastectomy in the wake of a stage one breast cancer diagnosis
She vividly remembers the chill from her spilled drink as it snaked its way inside the compression garment she was wearing as part of her recovery process

The sudden dampness came as a shock — not because it was unpleasant, but because she never expected to feel anything in that area at all, certainly not so soon after surgery.  Key takeaways Every year, hundreds of thousands of women in the United States are diagnosed with breast cancer and undergo mastectomies that can leave them with little to no feeling in their chests
In December 2025, the FDA cleared the da Vinci single-port surgical system for robot-assisted breast cancer surgery, specifically nipple-sparing mastectomies
Some surgeons are embracing this new technology because it offers a smaller, hidden scar and a clearer view inside the breast
Some patients also report better sensation in the chest area afterward

But critics say that there isn’t conclusive long-term evidence yet that robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies are as good as open mastectomies at making sure the cancer doesn’t come back, even if they are technically safe to perform
As Brasure knew, many people who get mastectomies are left with little to no feeling in their chests

That loss of sensation can affect a patient’s psychological well-being, sometimes actively alienating them from their bodies as they adjust to life after treatment.  “Every patient will have their own surgical goals
And mine was to look and feel as close as I did to how I looked and felt before I went into that operating room,” Brasure told me

Lucy De La Cruz, chief of breast surgery at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, offered Brasure the chance to be the hospital’s first patient to undergo a surgery that deployed a new robotic nipple-sparing mastectomy technique, she was enthusiastic

Especially because it was a procedure that some surgeons and studies have suggested leads to better preservation of feeling.  Using a robot to aid a mastectomy is not entirely novel — surgeons around the world have been experimenting with this technique for the past decade.  But what is new is that De La Cruz’s novel surgical plan combined several procedures into one operation
Using the da Vinci single-port robotic surgical system , she removed the breast tissue while preserving the nipples and skin
In the same operation, her team checked the lymph nodes, reconstructed the breasts with implants, and reconnected the nerve to the nipples to help restore sensation
In most robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies, the surgical incision is made along the armpit or the side of the chest
But here, De La Cruz and her team did everything through a single, 4-centimeter incision on each breast, naturally hidden under its fold
The hidden surgical scar and shorter recovery period, along with the possibility of having sensation back in her breasts post-surgery, were alluring for Brasure
Normally, surgeons performed nipple-sparing mastectomies through more conventional “open” techniques, typically through a long incision at the bottom of the breast
It is a technically challenging operation

Breast tissue extends all the way up to the collarbone, and surgeons have to reach it through a tight space with limited visibility, relying on their hands and eyes to look and feel their way around the breast

An assistant often uses large metal retractors to lift the skin around the incision to keep the area exposed and visible.  The procedure also carries a known risk of injury to the skin and nipple, sometimes severe enough that patients can lose the nipple and surrounding skin
These challenges led some surgeons to explore whether a robot-assisted surgery could help mitigate certain risks of open nipple-sparing mastectomies

But it was only in December 2025 that the Food and Drug Administration specifically cleared the use of the da Vinci single-port machine to perform mastectomies in the United States.  And at least for Brasure, it seems to have made all the difference, helping her feel better connected to her body after a procedure that might, under other circumstances, have left her with a radically altered sense of it
In theory, robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies sound like an amazing example of where surgical technology can take us
The American Cancer Society estimates that, in 2026, about 321,910 new cases of invasive breast cancer will be diagnosed in women

Many women opt for mastectomies not just as an active cancer treatment but also preventatively to reduce their risk, especially when they have a BRCA mutation — which indicates a very high likelihood of developing breast cancer — or a family history of the disease

A surgery with the potential to preserve more sensation, leave fewer surgical scars, and allow patients to recover more quickly promises to be a boon to women’s health.  Instead, robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies have proved extraordinarily divisive among oncological surgeons
Some, including De La Cruz, have embraced them
Others worry that the technology has gotten ahead of the evidence, especially on one of the most important measures in cancer treatment: making sure that the cancer doesn’t come back

The case for robotic mastectomies Maleeha Aziz, a 33-year-old deputy director at an abortion fund in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, grew up around breast cancer.  Aziz was 3 years old when her mother was first diagnosed

As a child, even though she couldn’t completely understand what was happening, she remembers her mother slowly losing her luscious, thick hair and how she could no longer pick Aziz up after the double mastectomy surgery.  It was clear that there was a family history, and Aziz felt like the cancer wasn’t skipping a single person
Her nani, or maternal grandmother, and her aunt had been diagnosed with ovarian and breast cancer, respectively

But the last straw was when her 32-year-old cousin — as close to her as a sister — received a stage three breast cancer diagnosis while she was pregnant.  Having seen the ravages of the disease firsthand and knowing from genetic testing in her early 20s that she was a BRCA carrier, Aziz ultimately decided that it would be better to get a preventative double mastectomy and reduce her cancer risk rather than live with pervasive anxiety from screening to screening.  “Preventative care is not radical
What is radical is to get cancer,” she told her family when they worried that it was an unnecessary medical intervention
A preventative mastectomy can lower the risk of breast cancer by close to 90 percent .  Aziz, like Brasure, was keen on sensation preservation

She remembered hating the numbness on her abdomen after her C-section delivery when she had her daughter, and couldn’t imagine the same around her breasts.  So in 2023, at the age of 29, Aziz opted for a preventative robotic nipple-sparing mastectomy at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center as part of surgical oncologist Dr
Deborah Farr’s study on the feasibility of using the da Vinci single-port machine to perform the procedure

title: The good news about homelessness comes with a catch
excerpt: Tents belonging to homeless people are set up between Schleusenkrug and Bahnhof Zoo in the Charlottenburg neighborhood, next to an S-Bahn line. | Marion van der
body: Tents belonging to homeless people are set up between Schleusenkrug and Bahnhof Zoo in the Charlottenburg neighborhood, next to an S-Bahn line. | Marion van der Kraats/picture alliance via Getty Images On a cold winter night in January, social workers and volunteers in towns and cities across the country fanned out to look for anyone living without shelter — on benches, on trains, on steps outside churches, in tents below underpasses
The goal of this national ritual is to get an accurate estimate of how many homeless people are out there each year

Combined with additional data on people staying in shelters, it’s the basis for the US Department of Housing and Urban Development’s Point-in-Time Count , the federal government’s benchmark number.  And there’s some good news in this year’s count, which HUD preliminarily released this month
Trump administration officials announced that 698,425 people were homeless on a single night in January, down 6.3 percent from a year earlier
HUD released the number ahead of its full annual report to Congress, but if it holds, it would be the largest one-year drop since national counts began in 2007
A separate analysis commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness (NAEH) estimated a similar 6.7 percent decline
Key takeaways Preliminary federal data shows homelessness down 6.3 percent, which would be the biggest one-year drop since 2007
Fewer migrants, slower rent growth, and local programs all likely helped, but no one knows how much
Chronic homelessness, the focus of Trump’s overhaul, barely changed
It marks the second straight year the national homelessness count has fallen
Homelessness had climbed by about a third between 2022 and 2024, hitting a record of about 771,000 people in 2024, then fell to 745,652 in 2025

But there are also competing stories as to what’s behind the positive trend, as well as the more persistent trouble spots, that pit the White House and housing advocates against each other, with each favoring very different policy approaches

The stakes are high for them to get it right — while homelessness is declining nationwide, the number of people who have been homeless for prolonged periods and often face especially dire challenges has remained stubbornly high

Why are there fewer homeless people in 2026? The Trump administration and homeless advocates point to different explanations to account for the recent drop.  “President Trump’s actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner told Vox in a statement
Both sides agree that the rapidly decreasing number of newly arrived migrants is a part of the story

The asylum-seekers who crowded into shelters in Boston, Chicago, Denver, and New York City in 2023 and 2024 are mostly gone now, and economists at the University of Chicago and Dartmouth estimated that asylum-seekers accounted for about 60 percent of the jump in shelter counts during those two years
Every expert I talked to said their departure explains at least part of this year’s national drop
Slower rent growth, a stronger job market, and communities recovering from disasters like Hurricane Helene and the Maui fires likely helped, too

While fewer people are homeless than a year ago, per the new Point-in-Time survey, HUD’s annual count notoriously excludes many people without a stable home , like those doubled up with relatives or living week to week in motels

But the heart of the dispute between the White House and advocates are chronically homeless people, meaning those who’ve been homeless for at least a year, or repeatedly over a three-year period, and have a serious mental illness or addiction
Their numbers seem to have barely budged in the NAEH’s review

Turner blames “failed Housing First policies” — the approach of giving people permanent housing without first requiring them to get sober or enter treatment — for keeping homelessness so high in the US

In this telling, tough love is needed to get troubled individuals to the point where they can live independently, including clearing makeshift camps and using the threat of criminal punishment to get people to accept help from social services.  Homeless advocates see things differently, favoring programs that aim at getting people shelter first and then using that as a stable base for them to receive additional services
They credit the 2026 decline to the same local programs and permanent housing policies the Trump administration wants to cut

The NAEH said that while there are many reasons for the drop, it’s “abundantly clear” that “homeless services systems and providers nationwide are successfully using their limited resources to reach people in need.” The advocates also point to veteran homelessness, which has fallen by nearly 60 percent since 2010 under the “Housing First” model , including another 7.8 percent this year as evidence their approach yields sustainable results if properly funded

Ann Oliva, the CEO of the National Alliance to End Homelessness, noted the administration hasn’t significantly changed its approach to veterans “because it’s been working.” She also told me the national decline was “quite broad based,” showing up in cities that sheltered large numbers of migrants as well as in places that didn’t

The debate over what’s driving the decline comes as lawmakers, advocates, and the courts fight over the future of homelessness policy — and which competing programs limited pools of funding should go toward.  In 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that cities can punish people for sleeping outside even when there aren’t enough shelter beds for them, and hundreds of cities and more than a dozen states have since passed or stepped up enforcing camping bans

Since taking office, President Donald Trump has gone further, attacking Housing First policies and trying to steer federal homelessness money away from permanent housing and toward short-term housing and treatment programs

His administration has repeatedly lost in court, most recently last week, when a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down HUD’s plan to set aside $1.3 billion of this year’s roughly $4 billion in homeless grants for short-term programs
The ruling means programs that already provide permanent housing can compete for that money again, and HUD has until the end of the year to distribute the funds
All the back-and-forth has been hard on the people running these programs
In a survey by NAEH, nearly half of local homelessness leaders said the uncertainty over federal money had already led programs in their area to cut services or shut them down
Why is chronic homelessness stuck? Chronically homeless people are often the hardest to move into permanent, stable housing
Most are poor and have a serious mental illness or addiction, and many have criminal records that make landlords balk at renting to them
And if they do manage to find a place to live, they often need ongoing supportive services to keep it
Their numbers hit a record high in HUD’s 2025 report, at 155,750 people nationwide, with over 40 percent of them living in California
HUD didn’t release a preliminary figure for chronic homelessness this month, but NAEH estimates it rose about 1 percent in 2026
Their estimate’s margin of error includes a small decline, so it’s not yet clear whether chronic homelessness changed at all this year
Oliva, NAEH’s CEO, argues that a big part of why chronic homelessness is stuck is that communities don’t have enough housing
Her organization estimates there was enough permanent housing for only about 9 percent of people who were homeless during the 2025 count

title: A Little The Crucible . A Little The Craft . A Lot of Catholic Guilt.
excerpt: The new Netflix show’s title card bears its name in a Gothic typeface—fittingly monastic for a series set in a Catholic high school
body: The new Netflix show’s title card bears its name in a Gothic typeface—fittingly monastic for a series set in a Catholic high school

But upon closer look, the imposing script is specifically referencing a more modern aesthetic: the rhinestone-studded Juicy Couture logo, frequently seen in the early aughts emblazoned across the backsides of velour tracksuits

That choice, however, is startlingly apropos: The Body , set in 2004, is as much concerned with girlhood—and all of its material obsessions and hormonal impulses—as it is with the religious experience
Here, in fact, these often seem to be considered one and the same

The show, a mix of campy horror and psychodrama, has topped the streaming charts; it has also earned the ire of some viewers who consider its premise blasphemous—the story of a Catholic school’s girls’ dance team called the Lions, whose members reckon with their beliefs in the fallout of a traumatic event: In the series premiere, the teens lead an Ecstasy-powered, mock-satanic hazing ritual at a Halloween party, after which one new member, Grace (played by Sofia Wylie), has several seizures
She then dies but somehow comes back to life—what one girl drolly describes as a Jesus-like resurrection

As Grace lies comatose, her teammates question whether her condition is the result of Satan preying on them for invoking his name during the initiation, and whether the “visions” they each start having are the result of mass hysteria; the series makes a valid case for both possibilities
The Body revels in the teens’ more garden-variety exploits as well, in explicit scenes (back-seat sex, raunchy drawings) that are par for the course with today’s teen dramas

The difference here, however, is that this show often depicts messing with drugs and messing with the devil as equally dangerous adolescent acts of rebellion. [ Read: The Americans having the most sex ] Most of the Lions initially treat Catholicism as a joke, and they want everyone else to see them laughing
One girl sports a tight-fitting T-shirt that reads Jesus saves
Before the Halloween party, the co-captain Elise (Sara Boustany) warns the other dancers that donning provocative schoolgirl costumes is “redundant.” The event itself is held at what the St
Mark’s students call the “Devil’s House,” an abandoned convent whose former inhabitants are rumored to have lost their minds
The night offers the teens a chance to flip a symbolic middle finger to a religious institution that demands their subservience
Defiance is a form of self-control, and they exercise it in the most extreme ways possible
But after Grace seemingly begins to haunt her teammates, the girls’ faith takes on a visceral—even punishing—quality
Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), the outsider classmate who once spoke in tongues before forcing her way on to the dance team, encourages the teens’ mounting fears of divine persecution
In response, they each begin confessing their sins, religious and social. (“I made out with Katie’s dad!” one of them admits

Another shouts that she’s “part of the fucking chess club!”) What’s really pouring out in these girls’ revelations, however, is all of the pent-up steam that can accumulate for a teen stuck in a Catholic-school hothouse
The girls have long been fed a diet of mixed messages when it comes to their physical and emotional selves
Their teachers tell them that their bodies are temples they should keep pure
Pop culture, meanwhile, tells them that their bodies are tools of pleasure
They’ve been raised in the era of postfeminist girl power —the Spice Girls likely soundtracked their elementary-school years—and absorbed the notion that their destiny is theirs to control
But their faith, in the show’s rendering, still shoves women toward the back
It’s no wonder that when the Lions begin to suspect that they can directly affect their own lives, they crack
Their identities, the show seems to argue, are inextricable from the rules, rituals, and cultural influences that dominate their lives
The Body , then, works as a study in what happens when young women break from the strictures that keep them in line
These characters feel as ecstatic as saints and as tortured as martyrs, sometimes in the same hour—being a teenage girl has room for all expressions of faith.
